strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (expressiveness vs. inference efficiency of generative policies in offline RL) and grounds it in a coherent ODE flow-map perspective that cleanly connects consistency models, CTMs, shortcut models, and mean flows.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on D4RL Gym and AntMaze with 5 seeds, mean±std reporting, and code promised; the BC setting (Section 5.1) is a nice experimental design that isolates policy expressiveness from value guidance, and the AntMaze gains of GTP-BC (66.3 vs. 44.1 for C-BC) are substantial.

Ablations cover the two claimed contributions (score approximation and variational guidance) and go further, testing teacher-free alternatives (shortcut-style self-consistency, Mean Flow identity), which strengthens the design choices.

Theoretical support is provided: Theorem 1 bounds the gap between the surrogate-supervised and solver-supervised objectives by O(h^p), with a full proof in Appendix B.3, and the advantage-weighted objective derivation (Appendix B.5/B.6) is correct and connects properly to AWR-style variational RL.
Honest acknowledgment of limitations, e.g., remaining substantial training time and the impracticality of teacher-free JVP-based objectives under GPU settings.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the 'unified ODE solution map' framework is essentially the CTM (Kim et al., 2024) reparameterization extended with a general (t,s) pair; the two losses (instantaneous flow + trajectory consistency) mirror CTM's denoising + consistency losses. The value-guidance component is exponential advantage weighting (AWR/CRR) applied to a generative loss, closely paralleling QGPO, D-QL, and C-AC. The contribution is a combination and adaptation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

There is a narrative-implementation gap: the paper sells 'learning the entire solution map of the underlying ODE,' but the practical training samples straight-line pairs a_t = a + t·z with a shared z, so supervision is on straight conditional paths (consistency-training style), not the marginal PF ODE trajectory. Theorem 1 justifies this asymptotically, but the headline claim overstates what is actually learned, and the theorem's h (solver step size) refers to a solver never used in practice, weakening the theory-practice link.

Some reported numbers are anomalously high relative to the D4RL literature, raising evaluation concerns: e.g., BC on hopper-m of 83.7 and hopper-mr of 100.5 (typical BC values are roughly 50 and 10-20), and Table 2 antmaze-u = 100±0 over 5 seeds. Combined with per-task hyperparameter tuning shown in Table 4 (per-task learning rate, η, gradient norm), this suggests heavy per-task tuning that may undermine the generality claim and invites re-verification.

The central 'efficiency' claim is only weakly supported: the inference-time ablation (Appendix D.1) is on a single task, and GTP with T=5 (0.94 ms) is only modestly faster than diffusion at the same step count (1.16 ms) while slower than consistency models (0.55 ms). The efficiency advantage over well-tuned one/two-step baselines remains arguable.

Several baseline entries are missing in Table 2 (BDM and C-AC on antmaze-lp/ld), average rows lack standard deviations, and Adroit/Kitchen appear in the hyperparameter table but with no reported results; the efficiency-vs-performance trade-off claim would benefit from a broader sweep over inference steps K.

Training cost remains high (~4.3 h on one task on an RTX 4090-class GPU), and the practical advantage over the strong λ=0.01 linear-Q baseline (111.4 vs. 112.2) is small on the one task where the baseline did not diverge, so the necessity of the variational machinery is demonstrated more by robustness across seeds/tasks than by average performance.

strengths: The paper frames generative policies for offline RL through the lens of learning an ODE flow map, and the attempt to connect diffusion, flow matching, consistency models, CTMs, shortcut models, and mean flows under one notation (Section 3, Appendix B.1) is pedagogically useful and mostly well written.

The empirical evaluation is broad: behavior-cloning (Table 1) and actor-critic (Table 2) results on D4RL Gym and AntMaze over 5 seeds, with GTP reporting strong averages (89.0 Gym, 80.6 AntMaze) against a good set of baselines including D-QL, QGPO, and Consistency-AC.

The ablations are thoughtfully designed beyond standard component removals: they test the score approximation against an actual ODE solver (Table 3), compare teacher-based versus teacher-free (shortcut / identity-based) actor losses (Table 6, Appendix D.2), and include a multi-goal visualization (Figure 5) that directly probes the multimodality claim.

The variational advantage-weighted objective (Section 4.2) is practically sensible, and the comparison to linear Q-terms with divergence analysis (Appendix B.6) gives useful engineering insight for combining critics with generative policies.
Implementation details (hardware, hyperparameters, dynamic timestep scheduling in Appendix C) and a claimed code release support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result appears incorrect. In Theorem 1's proof chain, Lemma 2 bounds only the conditional *mean* of the one-step solver difference as O(|Δ|^p+1); the fluctuation term Δ(f̃ − f⋆) is a zero-mean random variable of size O(Δ) (since (x − E[x|x_t]) has variance independent of the step size). Proposition 1 (Eq. 46) then incorrectly asserts E‖S[f⋆](X̃) − S[f̃](X̃)‖ = O(|Δ|^p+1); the expectation of the *norm* of an O(Δ) zero-mean perturbation is O(Δ), and these perturbations accumulate to O(1) over the horizon. Consequently the claimed O(h^p) objective gap is not established, and the 'asymptotic equivalence to the ideal objective' claim is unsupported. This matters because the theory is presented as a headline contribution ('two key theoretically principled adaptations').

The theorem is also misaligned with the actual method: Theorem 1 justifies the surrogate in the limit h → 0, but in practice the intermediate points are sampled directly from the straight-line path (Eq. 11) with maximal jumps — precisely the regime where the bound is vacuous. Notably, the ablation shows the surrogate (112.2) *outperforms* the 'ideal' ODE-solver target (99.7), which contradicts the framing of the solver objective as the ideal and suggests the theory does not capture what actually drives performance.

Limited methodological novelty. Learning the full time-conditional flow map Φ(x_t, t, s) is exactly the Consistency Trajectory Model parameterization (Kim et al., 2024), and applying consistency/flow-map models as offline RL policies with a critic was done by Ding & Jin (2024). The two 'key adaptations' reduce to (i) straight-line consistency-training supervision (standard) and (ii) exponential advantage weighting (AWR, Peters et al. 2010). The paper is therefore best read as CTM + advantage-weighted BC, and the contribution rests mainly on empirical results.

The advantage-weighting theory is overextended: Theorem 2's derivation is valid only for log-likelihood losses, but the paper asserts the weighting 'directly applies to any generative training loss' (diffusion/flow-matching objectives), which does not follow — weighting a score-matching loss by exp(ηA) is not equivalent to matching π*. The practical truncation of negative advantages (Eq. 14) also deviates from the stated optimal solution without analysis.

Missing experimental details undermine reproducibility and trust in the results. How goal conditioning is handled for AntMaze — critical for interpreting the surprising GTP-BC scores of 85.0 on antmaze-md and 74.4 on antmaze-mp without any value guidance (Table 1) — is never explained in the main text. Baseline rows in Table 1 report no standard deviations despite the caption claiming 'mean and standard deviation'. Table 4 lists hyperparameters for 'Adroit and Kitchen tasks', yet no Adroit or Kitchen results appear anywhere in the paper.

The headline claims are inflated relative to the evidence: 'perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks' is supported by exactly one task (antmaze-u, 100±0); the efficiency-resolution claim is weakened by GTP using T=5 steps versus consistency's T=2 (0.94ms vs 0.55ms), which shifts rather than resolves the expressiveness–efficiency trade-off; and the efficiency ablation covers a single task (halfcheetah-medium-expert).

Several presentation and rigor issues: incomplete sentence at the end of the contributions ('will be released'); an indexing typo in Eq. (15); ablations for the variational guidance and score approximation confined largely to one task (hopper-medium-expert); and only a single-sentence limitations discussion (training time) in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: how to obtain generative policies for offline RL that are both expressive and fast at inference. The proposed answer (learning the full ODE solution map rather than only the map-to-origin, as in consistency policies) is a reasonable and well-motivated design point between Diffusion-QL and Consistency-AC.

The empirical evaluation is extensive for the main claims: behavior-cloning expressiveness (Table 1), full offline RL results (Table 2), inference-cost ablation (Table 5), teacher-free alternatives (Table 6), and a multi-modal visualization (Figure 5). Reported gains, especially on AntMaze (66.3 BC average vs 44.1 next-best; 80.6 RL average vs 78.3 QGPO), are substantial and, if reproducible, meaningful.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough for this area: the score-approximation ablation, the linear-Q-term baseline (with divergence analysis), and the teacher-free (Shortcut/Mean Flow) comparisons in Appendix D.2 directly test the paper's design decisions rather than only the final method.

The supplementary material is extensive, covering derivations, proofs, hyperparameters (Table 4), and implementation details including hardware, which supports reproducibility. The authors are candid about failure modes (divergence of identity-based and linear-Q variants) and honest about remaining limitations (e.g., substantial training time).
The paper is generally well written, with a clear narrative from the unified ODE view (Section 3) to the two practical adaptations (Section 4), and Figures 1-3 genuinely aid understanding.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core machinery is assembled from existing components: the flow-map reparameterization ϕ is explicitly 'inspired by' CTMs (Kim et al., 2024), and the paper itself concedes that CMs, CTMs, Shortcut Models, and Mean Flows are all instances of the same flow-map framework. Theorem 2's advantage-weighted objective is the standard KL-regularized/advantage-weighted BC result (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018) restated for generative losses. The genuine contribution is thus a specific combination (flow-map actor + advantage weighting + data-anchored surrogate supervision), which is incremental relative to Consistency-AC and Q-weighted variational diffusion work.

Theorem 1, a headline 'theoretically principled' claim, appears to have a flawed proof. The proof bounds E[S[f*](X̃k) − S[f̃](X̃k)] (a signed expectation, O(|Δk|^{p+1}) via Lemma 2) but then uses this to control E||·|| in the recursion (Eq. 47). The one-step difference contains Δk(f̃ − f*), whose norm is O(Δk), not O(Δk^{p+1}); only its conditional mean is O(Δk^{p+1}). Since f̃(xt,t) = (xt−x)/t uses a single sample while f* uses E[x|xt], the gap includes an irreducible posterior-variance term (O(1) in the squared objective) that does not vanish as h→0. The claimed |L_prac − L_ideal| = O(h^p) therefore appears unjustified without additional assumptions (e.g., vanishing conditional variance or averaging over samples). This undercuts the 'theoretically grounded adaptation' framing, though the practical scheme is still defensible empirically.

Credibility concerns in the results. GTP-BC achieves hopper-medium-replay = 100.5 and hopper-medium = 83.7 under pure behavior cloning, far above TD3+BC (60.9, 59.3) and beyond what is typically reported for any BC-style method on these datasets; antmaze-umaze gives 100±0 with zero variance over 5 seeds. These outliers warrant per-task analysis or additional evidence.

Internal inconsistencies. The hyperparameter table (Table 4) caption references 'Adroit and Kitchen tasks' that never appear in the paper, and lists hyperparameters for only three of the six AntMaze variants evaluated. Table 2's C-AC and BDM columns contain missing entries for large AntMaze, complicating the average comparison. Table 1 claims 'mean and standard deviation over 5 random seeds' but baseline entries have no std (presumably copied from prior work), which should be stated explicitly.

The efficiency claim is narrower than the framing suggests. GTP uses K=5 sampling steps while consistency baselines use K=2, and the measured inference time (0.94 ms vs 0.55 ms) shows GTP is only 'moderately slower'; the claim of 'resolving' the expressiveness-efficiency trade-off is more a favorable operating point than a resolution, and no wall-clock comparison on the more relevant AntMaze tasks is provided.

Key ablations (Tables 3, 5, 6) are confined to a single task (hopper-medium-expert / halfcheetah-medium-expert); given the strong AntMaze claims, ablations there would substantiate the central claims more convincingly.

The 'unified framework' of Section 3 is largely a re-description of known equivalences (denoiser ↔ infinitesimal flow map, self-consistency ↔ compositionality); its value is expository rather than a new theoretical insight, and the paper overstates it as a 'theoretical foundation' enabling the method.

strengths: The paper is technically solid overall. The unified ODE flow-map framework (Section 3) is clearly articulated, and the connection of prior methods (CMs, CTMs, Shortcut Models, Mean Flows) as instances/limits of the flow map Φ is well explained, including a genuinely useful derivation of a continuous-time identity-based alternative in Appendix B.2.

Theorem 4.1 (surrogate score approximation) is supported by a complete proof in Appendix B.3 (Lemmas B.1–B.2, Propositions B.3–B.5), and the assumptions (Lipschitz fields, zero-stable p-th order solvers, bounded moments) are standard and stated explicitly.

Empirical evaluation is comprehensive: D4RL Gym and AntMaze with 5 seeds (Tables 1–2), comparisons against recent generative-policy baselines (Table 5), OGBench and visual-observation tasks (Table 6), sampling-step and scheduling ablations (Tables 7–8), sensitivity analyses for T and η (Figure 6), and a matched compute comparison (Table 9). This is well above the typical ablation depth for this area.

The ablation on teacher-free objectives (Appendix D.7, Table 10) is honest and informative: the authors report that Shortcut-style and Mean-Flow-style losses diverged or degraded under PyTorch/GPU, and candidly attribute part of this to implementation constraints rather than overclaiming superiority of their teacher-based design.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: hyperparameters per task (Table 4), timestep schedule formula (Eq. 76), hardware details, and a public code link are provided.
A thoughtful impact statement discusses dataset bias and safety considerations for offline-learned policies.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. The core technical ingredients are largely assembled from existing components: the flow-map parameterization and surrogate ϕ is explicitly adopted from CTMs (Kim et al., 2024); the score/teacher approximation reduces supervision to straight-line paths, closely mirroring Consistency Training; and the value-driven objective (Theorem 4.4 / Eq. 14) is standard exponential advantage-weighted BC (cf. AWR, AWAC, and Q-weighted variational objectives of Ding et al., 2024). The novelty lies mainly in the specific combination and the stability analysis, not in fundamentally new principles.

The headline claim in the abstract that GTP achieves 'perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks' is an overclaim: Table 2 shows a perfect score only on antmaze-umaze (100±0), which FQL also attains (Table 5), and performance on the harder large-maze tasks (53.5, 71.0) still trails some baselines. The paper would be stronger with more precise claims.

The practical relevance of Theorem 4.1 to the actual algorithm is somewhat indirect: the proved objective (Eqs. 8–9) uses multi-step solver propagation, whereas the implemented consistency loss (Eq. 17) samples intermediate points directly as a_u = a + u·z (Eq. 11), i.e., straight-line segments. The theorem therefore justifies an idealization of the training loss rather than the loss itself; the gap between the two is acknowledged qualitatively but not bounded.

Some experimental details are thin or borrowed: several baseline numbers in Tables 1, 2, and 5 are taken from prior papers (including some FQL results taken from the SSCQL paper), so compute and tuning budgets across methods are not fully controlled; SSCQL results are missing for all AntMaze tasks.

GTP does not resolve the expressiveness–efficiency trade-off as decisively as claimed: it remains slower to train than lightweight consistency methods (CAC: 3.7h vs GTP: 4.3h) and slower at inference than FQL (0.67–0.94 ms vs 0.36 ms), so its advantage is confined to policy quality (the paper does acknowledge this in D.6, but the framing elsewhere is stronger).

Several design choices (λ_Flow, dynamic timestep schedule s0/s1, per-task gradient-norm clipping values in Table 4) appear hand-tuned per task, which slightly weakens the claim of robustness without per-task tuning.

The unifying framework, while elegant, is presented with a large amount of expository material (Section 3, Appendix B.1) that largely re-derives known relationships, at the expense of a sharper statement of what is genuinely new.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is extensive: D4RL Gym and AntMaze with 5 seeds, additional OGBench and pixel-observation results, sensitivity analyses, computational-efficiency measurements (Table 9), and ablations covering the score approximation, value guidance, time scheduling, and teacher-free alternatives.

The core technical pipeline (flow-map parameterization from CTM-style surrogates, consistency + instantaneous losses, advantage-weighted generative training) is coherently assembled, and the reported results are strong, particularly on AntMaze (66.3 BC average, 80.6 RL average).

The ablations are unusually candid and informative: the paper honestly reports that teacher-free variants (Shortcut/Mean-Flow style) diverge or degrade, that the linear-Q baseline diverges, and that GTP is not the cheapest option (CAC trains faster). This transparency is appreciated.

The theoretical framing (Theorem 4.1 bounding the objective gap from the surrogate score by O(h^p)) provides at least a formal scaffold for the design choice, and the appendix derivation is worked out in detail.
An impact statement and a limitations discussion (training cost acknowledged in the conclusion) are included.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the central ideas. The 'unified ODE framework' of Section 3 is largely a restatement of the flow-map view already explicit in Consistency Trajectory Models (Kim et al., 2024) — the paper itself adopts the parameterization ϕ 'inspired by (Kim et al., 2024)' — and of the consistency/flow-matching equivalence discussed in Lu & Song (2025) and Mean Flows (Geng et al., 2025). The advantage-weighted objective (Theorem 4.4) is a standard AWR/KL-regularized result (Peters et al., 2010; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2019), and Q-weighted variational generative policies already exist (Ding et al., 2024, QIPO, which the paper cites and compares against). The contribution reduces to an incremental combination of known ingredients applied to offline RL, yet it is framed as a 'new and more general policy paradigm.'

Theorem 4.1 appears to formalize a degenerate case. The surrogate field f̃(xt,t) = (xt − x)/t is only defined on the straight line x + tz; a solver 'propagated' with f̃ from an on-line point stays on the line by construction (Euler with f̃ is exact there), so the O(h^p) gap statement essentially re-derives the conditional-expectation argument behind consistency training / flow matching. The proof also invokes Lemma B.1 (unbiasedness conditional on xt) at intermediate solver states, where the conditioning event differs — a gap that is not addressed. The strong assumptions (Lipschitz f⋆, zero-stability, bounded moments) are unverified for the actual neural policy.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The abstract states GTP achieves 'perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks,' but Table 2 shows a perfect 100 on exactly one task (antmaze-u). Similarly, 'state-of-the-art' holds only on averages: GTP loses on halfcheetah-m (53.9 vs. C-AC 69.1) and halfcheetah-mr, and on antmaze-lp it trails QIPO-Diff substantially (53.5 vs. 73.2). Marginal average gains over BDM/D-QL/IDQL-A (≈1–2 points on Gym) are not supported by significance testing, and many baseline entries lack reported standard deviations.

A tension exists between the claimed robustness and the actual hyperparameter treatment. The paper claims the variational guidance 'does not require per-task hyperparameter tuning,' yet Table 4 lists per-task η values (1.0 vs 5.0), per-task gradient-norm clipping, per-task Q-normalization and max-Q-backup flags — i.e., meaningful per-task tuning did occur.

The efficiency narrative is internally inconsistent. The paper motivates GTP by the expense of ODE-based training, yet the training schedule ramps discretization up to N = 1280 steps (Eq. 76); the 'w/o score approximation' ablation only restricts the solver to three steps, a weak version of the comparison; and Table 9 shows CAC is both faster to train (3.7h vs 4.3h) and faster at inference (0.55ms vs 0.94ms), leaving the headline expressiveness–efficiency story weaker than claimed.

Reproducibility concerns. The code-availability sentence is literally unfinished ('Our code is publicly available at' with no URL). OGBench results in Table 6 include a fixed '100' with no variance for cube-single, which is suspicious even for a task-average. Baseline numbers are aggregated from multiple sources with mixed evaluation protocols, and no statistical tests accompany any comparison.

The value-guidance mechanism inherits a known limitation that is under-discussed: with η = 0 the policy is BC, and improvement relies entirely on reweighting dataset actions by a critic trained with a standard TD loss using the generative policy in the bootstrap (Eq. 16). The paper does not analyze when this can fail (e.g., datasets where advantage weighting provides no coverage of near-optimal actions), beyond the single D4RL suite; the antmaze-lp result suggests such failure modes exist.

Presentation: Section 3 is verbose and spends considerable space re-deriving relations to prior models that the appendix then re-derives again; the framing of known results as numbered 'Theorems' (e.g., Theorem 4.4) inflates the perceived theoretical novelty.

strengths: The unified ODE flow-map perspective (Section 3, Appendix B.1) is a well-executed exposition that usefully connects diffusion, flow matching, consistency models, CTMs, Shortcut Models, and Mean Flows within a single parameterization, and clearly positions prior methods as special cases.

The paper identifies and addresses real practical obstacles (self-referential supervision instability, computational cost, objective misalignment) rather than only proposing a new loss; the teacher-anchored score approximation and advantage-weighted objective are well-motivated engineering contributions.

Theorem 4.1 provides a formal justification for the closed-form surrogate with a detailed proof (Appendix B.3), bounding the objective gap by O(h^p), and is complemented by an informative empirical ablation (Table 3) showing the approximation is both faster and more stable.

Empirical results are convincing and comprehensive: state-of-the-art generative-policy performance on D4RL (Gym avg 89.0, AntMaze avg 80.6), 5-seed mean±std reporting, additional comparisons with recent baselines (FQL, QIPO, SSCQL), OGBench and visual-observation evaluations, sensitivity analyses for T and η, computational cost comparisons, and a multi-goal visualization demonstrating multimodality.
Reproducibility is good: code is stated to be publicly available, hyperparameters are tabulated per task (Table 4), and hardware/protocol details are given.

The paper is honest about limitations (higher training cost than lightweight consistency methods, brittle teacher-free alternatives investigated in Appendix D.7), and includes a thoughtful impact statement.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited: the core parameterization ϕ is explicitly inspired by CTMs (Kim et al., 2024), the surrogate supervision with straight-line paths closely mirrors Consistency Training, and the value-guidance component (Theorem 4.4, Appendix B.5) is a standard variational RL/AWR result (Peters et al., 2010; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018) repackaged as a 'theorem'. The paper's contribution is primarily a careful adaptation of these ingredients to offline RL rather than a fundamentally new method.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 has a subtle gap: Lemma B.2 establishes the one-step surrogate bias vanishes only in conditional expectation given x_{τ_k}, but the local error term Δ_k(f̃ − f*) carries O(1) noise that does not vanish deterministically; the global recursion in Proposition B.3 implicitly treats the per-step error as an O(|Δ_k|^{p+1}) deterministic bias. A martingale/conditional-expectation argument over the full trajectory would be needed to make the O(h^p) bound rigorous as stated.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence: the abstract states 'perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks', but Table 2 shows a perfect 100 only on antmaze-umaze (the easiest of the six); other strong results are not perfect scores.

Gains on Gym are modest (89.0 vs. D-QL's 87.9, with e.g. halfcheetah-m and walker2d-mr below baselines), and some standard deviations are relatively large (e.g., antmaze-mp ±8.1), so the state-of-the-art claim rests mainly on the AntMaze suite; per-task hyperparameters (η, gradient norms in Table 4) suggest nontrivial tuning.

The unification exposition, while elegant, occupies substantial paper real estate without yielding testable predictions distinct from CTM/Mean Flow; the two 'theoretically principled adaptations' and their ablations are the actual novel content, and the framing could be more precise about this.
